slides.title: PITAS Infrastructure Rules
slides.lead: They hold for Assignments 8 to 11. Your final presentation assesses each objective against its “Achieved when” column, using these terms.
defs: A kind of shared service: WebSub hub, MQTT broker, pod server, identity provider (Solid-OIDC issuer) or discovery service
One running deployment of a component at its own address, e.g. the HiveMQ public broker
The party that decides what runs on an instance and can stop it

aside.alt: A frame labelled Operator: HiveMQ around a machine labelled HiveMQ cloud, which holds a green box labelled Instance of MQTT broker at broker.hivemq.com.
aside.caption: The notation of the following diagrams

slides.title: Who Operates an Instance?
slides.alt: Deployment diagram with one frame per operator. Top row: Google and Switchboard each run a WebSub hub, HiveMQ runs an MQTT broker, and the course runs the resource directory on its resource VM. Bottom row: Group 2 runs a PITAS app and an MQTT broker on its VM and a second MQTT broker on an extra VM; Group 5 runs a PITAS app on its VM.
slides.lead: Rule 1: a group operates its group VM and any extra VM the course gives it.
slides.notes: Top row: the outside providers Google, Switchboard, HiveMQ and the course. Bottom row: two of the six groups.

slides.title: Self-Hosted or Foreign?

callout.text: Who is a foreign provider for Group 5?

slides.alt: The deployment diagram of the previous slide, with one frame per operator: Google, Switchboard, HiveMQ, the course, Group 2 and Group 5. The two MQTT brokers on the VMs of Group 2 are green and marked self-hosted.
slides.notes: Ask the room first; the next slide shows the answer.
slides.lead: Rule 2: your own VMs are self-hosted. Rule 3: every other operator is a foreign provider.

slides.title: Self-Hosted or Foreign?

callout.text: Who is a foreign provider for Group 5?

slides.alt: The same diagram with the answer: the frames of Google, Switchboard, HiveMQ, the course and Group 2 are highlighted in teal and titled foreign provider. Only the frame of Group 5 keeps the title operator. The two MQTT brokers of Group 2 are still marked self-hosted.
slides.notes: Every operator except Group 5, Group 2 included (Rule 3). Group 2's brokers are self-hosted for Group 2 (Rule 2) and come from a foreign provider for Group 5.
slides.lead: Rule 2: your own VMs are self-hosted. Rule 3: every other operator is a foreign provider.

slides.title: When Does an Instance Count?
points: (b) it is reachable from every group VM
(c) a group other than its operator uses it in a demonstration
(d) if a group operates it, it runs on that group's VM or an extra VM from the course

aside.alt: Group 5's PITAS app uses an MQTT broker on the Group 2 VM, marked counts, and, through a tunnel, an MQTT broker on a Group 2 laptop, marked not counted.
aside.caption: Both brokers are listed and reachable. The one on the laptop fails (d).

paragraphs: Rule 4: an instance counts exactly when

slides.title: One Service, Several Components
points: Rule 5: a service counts once for each component it provides
A Community Solid Server (CSS) is both a pod server and an identity provider
You will learn more about the CSS in Assignment 9

aside.alt: On a course VM operated by the course, a Community Solid Server provides two interfaces: pod server and identity provider.

slides.title: Independently Operated

callout.text: Are the two MQTT brokers of Group 2 independently operated?

slides.alt: Google and Switchboard each run a WebSub hub in their own operator frame. Group 2 runs one MQTT broker on its VM and one on its extra VM, both inside the Group 2 frame.
slides.caption: The two WebSub hubs are independently operated.
slides.notes: No. Group 2 operates both of its VMs (Rule 1), so one party can stop both brokers.
slides.lead: Rule 6: different operators, so no single party can reconfigure or stop both.

slides.title: A Single Designated Instance
slides.alt: The PITAS apps of Groups 1 to 6 all point to one MQTT broker in the HiveMQ cloud, marked designated, with the note: the only counting MQTT broker.
slides.caption: Who operates it does not matter.
slides.lead: Rule 7: the only counting instance of a component, used by all six groups.

slides.title: A Fallback

callout.text: Which components have no fallback yet among the provided instances?

points: Rule 8: a second counting instance of the same component
Groups use it alongside the first instance, or switch to it by changing configuration only

aside.alt: Group 5's PITAS app uses four provided instances: the WebSub hub of Google, the WebSub hub of Switchboard, reached by a dashed arrow labelled alongside, or by configuration, the MQTT broker of HiveMQ and the resource directory of the course.

slides.notes: Ask the room first; the next slide shows the answer.

slides.title: A Fallback

callout.text: Which components have no fallback yet among the provided instances?

points: Rule 8: a second counting instance of the same component
Groups use it alongside the first instance, or switch to it by changing configuration only

aside.alt: The same diagram with the answer in colour: the WebSub hub of Switchboard is green, and the MQTT broker of HiveMQ and the resource directory of the course are teal.

slides.notes: Answer to the question: the MQTT broker (only HiveMQ) and the discovery service (only the course's resource directory). The WebSub hubs have a fallback: Google and Switchboard, once both count. A group can give the broker a fallback, e.g. a broker on its own VM that another group uses.
